topics.name: Engineering
topics.desc: How things are designed and built

article.title: Town to regain covered span lost to Irene
article.summary: The Bartonsville covered bridge in Rockingham, Vermont, became a symbol of Tropical Storm Irene's damage after a video showed it being swept down the Williams River. About a year later, the town was rebuilding it by hand, one beam at a time, using methods the original 1870 builders would have recognized. Residents had refused a modern steel-and-concrete replacement almost as soon as the old bridge was gone. The story shows how a small community's attachment to an old engineering design shaped how a failure was repaired.
facts: The old bridge was 152 feet long. The replacement was made longer, at 168 feet.
The 1870 bridge was built from timber cut in local forests, but the new bridge's wood came from the Pacific Northwest.
The video of the bridge washing away was shot by a Bartonsville native, Susan Hammond. Within hours, locals were already talking about rebuilding it.
The new span was assembled beside the river and moved into place afterward. A temporary bridge carried traffic in the meantime, and the crossing was to close for only about 45 days.
questions: When a beloved old structure fails, should it be replaced with the same design or with a modern one? What would you weigh?
Why might traditional timber-framing methods still be a good engineering choice today?
How does a small town's identity get tied up with a single piece of infrastructure?

related.t: Mars Hill/Lowell Observatory Truss Bridge: Bridge Technology (Northern Arizona University)
History of a Truss Bridge (Tennessee DOT)

alt.title: Vulcan Bridge in Vulcan
alt.summary: Vulcan, West Virginia, had one way in and out: a rickety swinging bridge. When the bridge rotted and collapsed, the town was cut off from the outside world. Local resident John Robinette named himself mayor and, after the state ignored him, asked the Soviet Union and East Germany for foreign aid to build a new one. The embarrassment of that request got the state to act, and the bridge was finally built with American money.
facts: Residents used a railroad maintenance path after the collapse. The railroad threatened to prosecute anyone it caught trespassing there.
Bomb threats were reportedly made against any bridge built with communist help.
A Soviet reporter, Iona Andronov, traveled to Vulcan to meet the mayor and look at the bridge site.
The replacement took about two years to finish, and it has only one lane. The mayor christened it with two bottles of Russian vodka.
questions: Why did a request to a rival superpower get action when ordinary appeals to officials did not?
Who decides which small-town infrastructure is worth building and maintaining, and how should the cost be weighed against the benefit?
What does a bridge failure cost a community beyond the structure itself?

article.title: China's Flowers, 1922-1949
article.summary: Austrian-American botanist Joseph Rock spent 27 years in China collecting thousands of plant samples before the Communist takeover pushed him out. The article describes his expeditions through Yunnan and nearby borderlands, including a 1925 ambush by bandits. It also shows that he was far more than a plant collector. He documented the languages, cultures and faces of the people he met, and his specimens are still used by botanists today.
facts: Rock and his entourage were ambushed by bandits while on a botanical expedition in Yunnan in 1925.
He wrote a 1,094-page Naxi–English dictionary, as well as two histories of the Naxi people.
National Geographic published many of his travel diaries between 1922 and 1935.
Researchers are now using his old specimens to work out what could be restored in the landscape today.
questions: Rock is remembered as a botanist, but he also documented languages and cultures. Is it fair to call him just a 'plant hunter'?
What can century-old herbarium specimens tell scientists today that new collecting trips could not?
How should we weigh the scientific value of early 20th-century expeditions against the political and colonial contexts they operated in?

related.t: William Purdom: The Forgotten Arnold Plant Hunter (Arnold Arboretum)

alt.title: A Man, a Plan, a Lemon, China: The Ballad of Frank Meyer
alt.summary: This profile follows Frank Meyer, a USDA agricultural explorer who trekked across China's interior in the early 1900s. He was a newspaper celebrity in his day. Today he is remembered mostly for the Meyer lemon, which the piece argues is an ironic way to remember him. His life ended abruptly in 1918, when he vanished from a ship heading to Shanghai.
facts: Newspapers of his day printed dashing portraits of Meyer in his sheepskin coat, hunting boots and walking stick.
He noticed the small potted lemon plant in 1908 because it fruited heavily for its size.
When Meyer first landed in China in 1905, fewer than a dozen soybean varieties were in cultivation, according to the USDA.
He disappeared from a ship bound for Shanghai in 1918 at age 42.
questions: Why might a plant hunter's best-known find be a minor one, like a houseplant lemon, rather than the work he considered most important?
What does it say about the era that a government agency sent lone explorers to search the world for useful crops?
How might the mystery around Meyer's death have shaped the way he is remembered?

related.t: Frank Nicholas Meyer Collection (USDA National Agricultural Library)

article.title: Why the wiggle in a crowd's walk can put a wobble in a bridge
article.summary: When London's Millennium Bridge opened to crowds in 2000, it swayed alarmingly. Mathematicians have since built better simulations of how people walk to explain why. Walkers on a swaying bridge tend to slip into step with it, because that is easier than resisting it. The result is a feedback loop that makes the swings bigger. The new model predicts the crowd size at which the wobble starts suddenly.
facts: Tests on the Millennium Bridge found the lurching only began once roughly 165 people were on it.
Pedestrians drift into lockstep with a swinging bridge because going with the sway takes less effort than fighting it.
The study was led by a Georgia State University mathematician and was reported in Science Advances.
A later study from the same group challenged the lockstep explanation, saying people were simply trying not to fall over.
questions: Why might it feel natural to match your steps to a moving surface, even when you don't mean to?
How should engineers and event planners account for crowds that act as one even though no one has coordinated them?
What other everyday situations might make a crowd move in unison without anyone deciding to?

related.t: Crowd motion experiment reveals why crowds synchronise footsteps (City University of Hong Kong)
Why do some bridges wobble? Blame the way pedestrians walk on them (Science)
Why too many walkers cause bridges to wobble and sway (Futurity)

alt.title: What to do if you're in a crowd of panicking people
alt.summary: Researchers who study crowds, partly to design safer public spaces, explain how people move when something frightens them. Normally we constantly track the speed and direction of the people around us and try to avoid collisions. Under threat, people grow more aggressive, fill the free space ahead, and then move chaotically as they search for more room. A crowd-science professor advises trying to calm down and assess the situation instead of running without thinking.
facts: In normal walking, people are constantly estimating how fast others nearby are moving and where they are heading.
Under panic, people stop minding bumping into others.
After the free space in their chosen direction fills up, movement turns chaotic as people hunt for gaps.
One expert's advice is to assess the situation rather than react, since running blindly has caused many serious injuries.
questions: Why do researchers hesitate to give fixed survival advice for crowd emergencies?
How might the layout of a public space change the way a frightened crowd behaves?
What is the difference between a crowd acting irrationally and a crowd that is trapped by its surroundings?

related.t: Behaviour and Mechanics of Crowd Crush Disasters (Risk Frontiers)

article.title: Brazen Heads: The Curious Legend Behind Fortune-Telling Automata
article.summary: Long before computers, medieval and Renaissance storytellers imagined brass heads that could answer any question put to them. The tales were pinned on famous scholars such as Roger Bacon, Robert Grosseteste and Albertus Magnus. They look like an early daydream of a chatbot oracle, but they appeared centuries after the men's deaths. The article follows how the legend was used for wonder, for prophecy, and later for politics.
facts: Stories of Roger Bacon's brass head only show up centuries after he died, and there is no record he ever built one.
Bacon was fascinated by early astronomical clocks, which were also made of brass and also gave information about the cosmos.
Albertus Magnus was said to have spent 30 years building a brass man that could answer anything, but in one version it was so chatty that his student Thomas Aquinas smashed it.
Robert Grosseteste was said to have made a head using 'astral science' to predict the future.
questions: Why might people in the Middle Ages have imagined an answer-giving machine as a talking head rather than as, say, a book?
The legends were attached to real scholars who were also suspected of being wizards. What does that say about how societies react to new knowledge and technology?
If Aquinas really did smash a head for talking too much, what would be the modern equivalent of a chatbot that talks too much?

related.t: Chatbots Decoded: Exploring AI (Computer History Museum)

alt.title: A Team of Researchers Brought the World's First Chatbot Back to Life After 60 Years
alt.summary: ELIZA, the 1960s program that made people feel heard by a computer, spread across early networks until the original version dropped out of sight. A group of researchers called Team ELIZA dug through MIT's archives and found a 1965 printout of the source code. They got it running again on an emulated old time-sharing system. The code also held a surprise: a hidden mode that let users change the program's rules while it ran.
facts: Weizenbaum's own secretary was so drawn to ELIZA that she once asked to be left alone with it.
A BASIC version of ELIZA appeared in Creative Computing magazine in 1977, just as home computers were arriving.
The rediscovered code had a hidden 'teacher mode', switched on by typing a plus sign.
That mode let users add, remove and change rules on the fly, a feature barely mentioned in Weizenbaum's published work.
questions: Why do you think a copy of the program became more famous than the original?
What does it mean that a chatbot could be reprogrammed live by its users? Is that closer to learning than we usually give ELIZA credit for?
What other pieces of early computing history might be quietly lost, and who should be responsible for saving them?

related.t: Chatbots Decoded: Exploring AI (Computer History Museum)
